Fed Governor Waller (December voter) doubles down, explicitly calling for a 50bp hike in December unless the Fed signals another hike will follow in January.

▪ Last week his bar was conditional: 50bp “should be considered” if October core CPI came in around 0.3% or higher. It did, for a third straight month.
▪ “I’m very, very concerned about inflation. It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”
▪ “If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions.” “You might need to, like, shock people.”
▪ He’s worried businesses and consumers are getting used to inflation around 3%.
▪ He wants the Fed to reverse all three of its 2025 rate cuts and possibly go further. With September’s hike having undone one, that means 4.25%–4.5%, or one 50bp move from today’s 3.75%–4%.

For now he remains an outlier with most officials calling for "steady" (Hammack) or "gradual" (Paulson) increases. It's also not the view of the leadership. New York’s Williams, the FOMC vice chair, said Tuesday “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action” when asked about a 50bp hike.

▪️ Housing starts jumped 9.9% to 1.309 million, the biggest gain since June, well above the 1.250 million consensus (Morgan Stanley’s 1.320 million was closest), though both September and August were revised down, September to 1.191 million from 1.221 million.

▪️ Building permits fell 7.4% to 1.295 million, the lowest since May 2020, well below the 1.377 million consensus.
▪️ Single-family permits fell 8.7%, the most since February 2021, to 772,000, the lowest since January 2023, down in all four regions (West -14.5%, the most since April 2020); the three-month average is the lowest since March 2023.
▪️ Completions rose 6.5% to 1.272 million, while units under construction edged down to 1.272 million, 442,000 below the October 2022 record.
▪️ The backdrop: NAHB builder sentiment fell to 25 in November, the lowest since April 2012, and Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.33% in October, the highest monthly average since November 2023.

@C_Barraud’s Wednesday Morning Brief contained an interesting post from @sentimentrader that fits with the outperformance of the S&P 500 vs the Nasdaq-100: while over half the Nasdaq 100 is in a bear market (54% of its stocks are down 20%+ from their 52-week highs), just 32% of the S&P 500 is. The 20-day average of that gap just crossed 18.5 percentage points. After past crossings, the S&P 500 was higher three months later only 3 of 10 times, averaging a 2.9% loss.

But as SentimenTrader notes, half of those signals came in 2000–02. So I rebuilt the gap from 2011 using The Trading Tools’ free breadth data (which is the history of the free data - a great resource).

▪️ The gap is now the widest since 2011. Its 20-day average hit 19.9 points Tuesday, above the 2022 tech-bear peak (16.9) and the 2012 peak (17.1). It widened again Tuesday to 60% vs. 35.7%.

▪️ The 18.5 line has been crossed only one other time since 2011, also this year, in August. After the August crossing, the S&P 500 was down 2.3% three months later and the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) was down 5.4%.

▪️ But lowering the bar to the widest 5% of readings (13.6 points), with each episode dated to its first close above that level, gives five finished signals: November 2012 (S&P 500 +6.7% three months later), March 2021 (+8.0%), January 2022 (−7.9%), February 2026 (+6.9%) and July 2026 (+4.7%).

▪️ So that’s 4 of 5 higher, averaging +3.7%, vs. +3.1% for all days since 2011.

The one loser, then, was January 2022, the start of that year’s tech bear market. Combine that with SentimenTrader’s history, where half the signals (and most of the damage) came in 2000–02, and the pattern seems to be that the gap has been a warning, but outside of tech busts it has been a buying opportunity.

In that regard, SentimenTrader notes the gap closes one of two ways: the Nasdaq recovers, or more S&P 500 stocks fall into bear markets. In all four good episodes, the Nasdaq’s bear-market share was lower three months later (sharply in 2012, 29% to 17%, and 2021, 18% to 10%; modestly in both 2026 episodes). In contrast, in 2022 the Nasdaq’s share climbed from 39% to 62%, and the S&P 500’s more than doubled, peaking at 47%.

Right now the Nasdaq’s share is still rising (46% at the August signal, 60% now), which signals continued caution.

It’s a small sample and not SentimenTrader’s exact signal, so treat it as context rather than a timing tool.

US import prices continue to boost inflation, rising 1.1% for a second straight month in October, well above the 0.7% Bloomberg consensus, with the AI hardware buildout driving a record jump in capital goods prices. Note, import prices exclude tariffs.

▪️ Headline +1.05%, roughly the same as September’s +1.06% (revised from +1.13%). BLS couldn’t publish year-over-year changes because October 2025 data were never collected, but using BLS’s own suggested approximation, import prices are up an estimated 9.1% from a year ago, which would be the most since June 2022.
▪️ Nonfuel import prices +0.80%, the most since April, though September was revised down to +0.51% from +0.73%. They’re up an estimated 6.4% year over year, the most since April 2022.
▪️ Fuel +3.6% after an upwardly revised +6.3%. Petroleum +3.7% and up 46.8% from a year ago (BLS did publish that one), just shy of May’s 48.3%.
▪️ AI trade: capital goods +1.5%, “the largest advance since the index was first published on a monthly basis in December 1988,” per BLS, and a 10th straight gain, led by computers, peripherals and semiconductors. Nonelectrical machinery, about a quarter of all imports, rose 1.7%, the most in monthly data back to 1992. Semiconductors rose 2.95% and are up an estimated 40% year over year, a record in data back to 2006.
▪️ China: import prices from China rose 1.4%, “the largest monthly advance since the index was first published in January 2004,” per BLS, and are up an estimated 4.5% year over year, the most since April 2022.
▪️ Exports +1.1% after an upwardly revised +2.4%. Export prices to Japan jumped 3.7%, the most since March 2022, and agricultural export prices are up 9.9% year over year, the most since November 2022.

The @dailychartbook nightly email had an interesting chart (via @randgroup) showing gold falling to a 52-week low even as gold ETF holdings sit at a record. The problem? Price is set by the marginal buyer/seller, and those aren't currently the buyers in the tonnage data.

The steady buyers are still there:
▪️ Central banks bought 321 tonnes in Q3, up 42% y/y and the most since Q4 2024, per the World Gold Council.
▪️ China’s central bank added 26 tonnes in October, its biggest monthly purchase in three years, in a month when gold fell about 7%.
▪️ Gold ETFs took in 211 tonnes in Q3, pushing holdings to a record.

But look closer, and the flows square with the price action:
▪️ ETF buying slowed sharply in October to 19 tonnes globally ($2.7B), about 73% below the Q3 pace, and US funds were net sellers.
▪️ Record holdings are a stock, not a flow. They keep setting records as long as there’s any net buying, however small.
▪️Central bank buying is also small relative to the market. Gold traded a record $361B a day on average in 2025, about 3,000 tonnes changing hands daily. October’s $2.7B of global ETF inflows was less than 1% of a single day’s volume, and central banks’ Q3 buying works out to about 5 tonnes a day.

So the price is being set by fast money:
▪️ Speculators cut their net futures longs by about 21 tonnes in the week to Nov. 3 alone, more than all global ETF inflows in October.
▪️ In September, managed money net longs fell 84 tonnes, more than four times October’s ETF inflows.
▪️ Physical buyers who react to price have pulled back too, with Q3 jewelry demand down 17% and bar and coin demand down 19%.

Is the link between gold and real rates that broke in 2022 reasserting itself?  Too early to say, but the evidence is there. Gold is now down 31.5% from its January record.

@C_Barraud’s Tuesday Brief included ZeroHedge’s post on Goldman’s 2027 oil outlook, “Adaption,” framed by ZH as warning of an oil glut.

And Goldman’s base case does call for a glut. It sees Brent averaging $88/bbl in 2027 and easing to $78 by December, as a 2M bbl/day surplus lowers its fair-value estimate from about $90 today to the high $70's by end-2027. Three drivers:

▪️ The market likely tipped into surplus in October already. Goldman estimates a 1.6M bbl/day surplus as Persian Gulf crude exports recovered to their 2025 average.
▪️ Gulf output keeps climbing. Goldman sees it rising nearly 4M bbl/day from October levels in 2027, with 3.8M bbl/day of new pipeline capacity bypassing Hormuz coming online over the next year.
▪️ Chinese demand has been scarred by the shock. Goldman thinks China’s oil demand peaked in 2025 as electric cars and trucks took share during the price spike.

But note, Goldman’s forecast is above where oil futures trade for almost every period. As of the November 13 close, 2027 Brent futures were at $81, $7 below Goldman’s $88. For the first quarter, Goldman is at $96 versus $86 in futures. For 2031 to 2035, it’s at $75 versus $67. The only period where Goldman is below the curve is 2028.

Part of the reason is how fast the war premium has collapsed. Brent hit $117.64 on October 30 and is down about 21% since, to roughly $93. Goldman estimates the war risk premium in Brent fell from $27 the Friday before the midterms to “only a few dollars” last week. It calls that premium “quite low” given the geopolitical risks. Its risks are two-sided:

▪️ Upside: Brent could average about $120, with peaks near $130, if renewed escalation keeps Gulf output 2.7M bbl/day below its 2025 average.
▪️ Downside: Brent could fall into the $60's if Gulf output overshoots and the 1M bbl/day disruption allowance in Goldman’s base case doesn’t materialize.

For consumers, though, crude is expected to normalize faster than refined products. Goldman sees U.S. retail gasoline easing to $3.70/gal by end-2027 from $4.00 now, and diesel to $4.60 from $6.10.

The takeaway: Goldman sees a glut, but its price forecasts aren’t bearish relative to market pricing. After a 21% drop, Goldman’s forecasts sit above what you can lock in on the futures curve today. Goldman says traders should lean toward buying when its risk-premium estimate is small, as it is now, and suggests long summer 2027 European gasoline as a hedge against renewed escalation.

St. Louis Fed’s Musalem (2028 voter)  gives the most aggressive guidance from a Fed official yet on how far and fast he sees the Fed needing to go: “several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027,” starting “soon.”

▪ The calendar: only three FOMC meetings come before spring (Dec. 8–9, Jan. 26–27 and March 16–17), so “several” hikes means at least one per meeting.
▪ “In my view, current policy is not yet restraining inflation.” He agrees with Chair Warsh’s description of the September hike as “removing a dose of accommodation.”
▪ He’s “not overly concerned” by the recent tightening of financial conditions, which he says was smaller than after Liberation Day or the start of the Middle East conflict. That’s a direct counter to Daly and Bowman, who see tighter conditions as a reason to go slower.
▪ Inflation: October CPI and PPI suggest October PCE inflation “could be 3.8% and 3.2%” for headline and core, with “three-month rates running above six-month rates for every major category.”
▪ Expectations are anchored “because markets expect that the FOMC will raise its policy rate within the next few months.” “Moving sooner, while inflation expectations are anchored, has a better chance of succeeding.”
▪ Like Warsh on Monday, he doesn’t see an AI productivity boom yet: “the economy does not yet appear to be in a high-productivity growth regime.”

Industrial production fell 0.43% in October, the most since January and a clear miss vs the +0.1% expected, but the drop came from utilities and energy, not factories: manufacturing rose for a second month to its highest level since March 2022 boosted by a jump in auto output.

▪️ Total -0.43%, the largest decline since January and the first since August (revised to -0.07%), after September was revised up to +0.73%.
▪️ Utilities -4.25%, the largest drop since January 2023, reversing September’s jump to a record. ZeroHedge points to the fourth-warmest October on record. Total energy output -2.52%, the largest drop since May 2020.
▪️ Mining -0.85%, with oil and gas extraction -1.97% (largest drop since January 2024), though drilling rose 3.20% to its highest since March 2024.
▪️ Manufacturing +0.28%, in line, on a 4.44% jump in motor vehicles and parts (most since February 2025). Excluding autos it slipped 0.07%.
▪️ Hi-tech output +2.05% to a record, with semiconductors +15.31% year-over-year. Business equipment +0.96% to its highest since 2018, and defense and space at a record.
▪️ Year-over-year, total +2.15% (most since September 2022) and manufacturing +2.18% (most since March 2022).
▪️ Capacity utilization 76.36% vs 76.8% expected, 3.0 points below its long-run average. Factory utilization 76.04%, the highest since May 2024.

Strip out the weather-hit utilities and energy, and the factory sector held up in October. Heads up: the Fed’s annual revision on November 24 rebases the indexes to 2022 and will revise this history.
